profile.reading:
This is the Alabama Supercomputer Authority's data center at 686 Discovery Drive in Cummings Research Park, Huntsville, Alabama, one of the largest research parks in the country and a hub for the region's aerospace, defense, and technology industries. The Authority was created by the Alabama Legislature in 1989 to provide information-technology resources and services supporting education, research, and economic development statewide. It operates both the Alabama Supercomputer Center itself and the Alabama Research and Education Network (AREN), which connects K-12 schools, community colleges, universities, libraries, and government agencies across Alabama, and has served as the lead of the AREN Consortium in the federal E-Rate program since 1998. The Authority installed its current high-performance computing system, known as ASA-X, in 2023.

The Authority is led by CEO Debra Wallace, who joined ASA in 2008 and was named to the top role on January 1, 2021, the organization's first female CEO and its first CEO promoted from within, bringing more than 30 years of experience in accounting, technical administration, and education. In January 2023, General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT) was awarded a five-year, $152 million contract, with two option years, covering cybersecurity, software development, high-performance computing support, enterprise network management, hybrid multi-cloud hosting, IT systems support, and broadband connectivity for the Authority, building on an existing 30-year partnership between GDIT and ASA. Wallace described the contract as supporting broadband and related services to more than 780 educational clients statewide.

No published capacity or power figure for the Huntsville data center appears on the Authority's own site or in any regulatory filing found. Third-party data center trackers have cited a capacity figure near 96 megawatts and, separately, an address in the nearby city of Madison rather than Huntsville, but that location claim appears to conflate Madison County, the county Huntsville and Cummings Research Park sit within, with the distinct city of Madison, Alabama, and neither the capacity nor the alternate location has been corroborated by the Authority's own materials. As a state-chartered authority serving public education and government clients rather than a commercial provider selling data center capacity, ASA has no obligation or apparent incentive to publish detailed technical specifications the way a commercial colocation operator would, and none currently exist in the public record. What is well documented is the Authority's history, leadership, its GDIT partnership, its confirmed Cummings Research Park address, and the 2023 ASA-X system upgrade, a solid institutional record even without a published megawatt figure.

reading:
The Alabama Supercomputer Authority is a state authority, not a company, and it is in this registry because a single state owned building in Huntsville has been continuously operating research computing for the whole of Alabama's public education system for nearly four decades. The Authority was established by the Alabama Legislature in 1989 with a mandate to provide information technology resources and services for the advancement of education, research and economic development in Alabama. It serves K-12 schools, public libraries, community colleges, universities and selected government agencies, and it runs the statewide Alabama Research and Education Network that connects them.

The building predates the Authority. The Alabama Supercomputer Center at 686 Discovery Drive, in Cummings Research Park in Huntsville, was built in October 1987 on land the City of Huntsville donated that year, two years before the legislature created the body that now runs it. The Authority states the building spans nearly 24,000 square feet. Its first system was a Cray X-MP, and the machine installed in October 2023, designated ASA-X, is the tenth in that unbroken line. Under one roof the site houses a security operations centre, a network operations centre, a data recovery centre, the data centre itself and the Authority's operations staff. A separate business office sits at 445 Dexter Avenue in Montgomery, and the building carries the name of the George C. Wallace Alabama Supercomputer Center.

What the Authority sells is closer to a public utility than to a commercial product. High performance computing is provided free of charge to faculty, staff and students at Alabama public schools and universities. The statewide network offers connections from 100 megabits to 10 gigabits per second. Cybersecurity services include content filtering and system scanning for school networks, and the Authority manages federal E-Rate funding applications on behalf of Alabama schools and libraries, which for many small districts is the difference between having usable internet access and not. In December 2022 GDIT was awarded a five year contract with two option years, reported at about $152 million, covering cybersecurity, software development, high performance computing support, network management, application development, hybrid multi cloud hosting, IT systems support and broadband connectivity, extending a working relationship of roughly three decades.

What is not published is the physical plant. The Authority states no critical IT load, no utility service figure, no generator or uninterruptible power supply rating and no board governance structure for the Huntsville building, and this registry records those as unknown rather than inferring them from the size of the machines installed.
